newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish opposition sees obstacles to snap polls.
newsitem.headline: Turkish opposition sees obstacles to snap polls.

text.p: Turkey's main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz said on Wednesday there were too many obstacles in the way of an early election to solve a government crisis over Islamist activism.

"Elections are the last resort in a democracy...all the alternatives have not been exhausted in this parliament," Anatolian news agency quoted Yilmaz as telling MPs from his conservative Motherland Party.

Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan had challenged the secularist opposition, divided by bitter feuds, to go to the polls to clear up months of uncertainty over army demands that the government launch a crackdown on religious activism.
Yilmaz said the current voting system would favour Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party.
"Going to elections with today's election law, population count and voting districts would be sabotaging democracy," he said.

Welfare narrowly won polls in late 1995 with 21 percent of the vote and rules in coalition with a secularist party. Analysts say the Islamists' slice of the vote may have increased since the last polls but exact figures are hard to come by.

Earlier, veteran left-wing leader Bulent Ecevit acknowledged that Yilmaz and another opposition figure had only loosely agreed to a plan to replace Islamist Erbakan's coalition with a secularist alliance.

"Yilmaz found the idea of a broad-based government too ambitious," Ecevit told MPs from his Democratic Left Party. He also said leftist rival Deniz Baykal had not given a clear reply in a round of talks on Tuesday to his call for a shadow government that would oust Erbakan.
The Islamist wing of the government has come under heavy fire from Turkey's secularist power centres, led by the influential army, for plans to introduce Islam into public life.
